correctness.rationale: Proof verifies the normalization, exact admissible domain and all boundaries. For \(0<p\le1\) strict concavity proves uniqueness. For \(p>1\), the hyperbolic-ratio derivative is strictly monotone unless \(p=2\); this proves at most one positive critical amplitude. Derivative endpoint signs plus exact endpoint comparison give all global cases and equality multiplicities. At \(p=2\) the objective is exactly quadratic in amplitude; at \(p>2\) the fourth-derivative expansion rigorously gives the square-root onset. The p=3 example is certified by an exact completed square. Bundled exact-rational and finite numerical checker passed 244035 assertions, but is not used as a substitute for infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Full primary-text review found the beta-shaped plant-temperature models and their variable-temperature numerical comparisons but not a theorem globally optimizing two equal-duration temperatures at fixed mean for every cardinal exponent. The derived exact optimizer, jump/continuum/continuous regime classification, and square-root onset are not explicit consequences of the published model formula or the sign of curvature alone. Targeted mathematical-index and wider literature searches yielded no stated equivalent theorem. This is a best-knowledge originality decision with explicitly documented residual priority risks, not a certificate of uniqueness.
residual_risks: General theorems on constrained two-point beta moments or symmetric Jensen gaps may imply the result under a different name; no exhaustive bibliographic coverage is asserted.

value.rationale: A standard biologically motivated cardinal-temperature curve is applied to an explicit equal-day/night time-budget setting, with all admissible means and model exponents classified. The exact exponent-2 boundary separates a finite jump to zero variance from a continuous square-root optimizer with an exceptional full continuum at equality. These sharp structural boundaries are not merely local Jensen-sign checks or numerical optimization of arbitrary parameters. The p=3 benchmark gives an exact 37.5% modeled rate difference; it is potentially useful for interpreting thermoperiodic model bias, while not claimed as field guidance.
